title: Data Models
summary: The way a database organizes data. Learn the main shapes — tables, documents, graphs — and how to pick one.

blocks.markdown:
A **data model** is how a database organizes data — the shape it stores things in and the rules for connecting them.

- It decides the **structure**, how you **query**, and what **rules** must hold.
- Match the shape to your data and questions stay simple.
- Databases are grouped by their model: relational, document, graph, key-value.
- **Relational** is the default; the others fit specific needs.

blocks.subTitle: The main families
blocks.markdown:
The shapes you'll meet.

| Model | Stores data as |
|---|---|
| Relational | Tables of rows |
| Document | JSON-like documents |
| Key-value | Key and value pairs |
| Graph | Nodes joined by edges |

Most real apps use two or three together.

Data comes in three shapes, and the model follows from it.

- **Structured** — fixed fields, same for every record. Fits **relational**.
- **Semi-structured** — self-describing, fields can vary per record (JSON). Fits **document**.
- **Unstructured** — raw blobs like images or text, no fields. Kept in files.

A **schema** is just the agreed set of fields and their types.

blocks.subTitle: Hierarchical
blocks.markdown:
The **hierarchical model** stores data as a tree: each record has one parent, and you read by walking down from the top.

- Good for **one-to-many** (one department, many employees).
- Weak at **many-to-many** — it forces duplicated data.

**Many-to-many:** each side links to many of the other, e.g. students and courses.

blocks.subTitle: Network
blocks.markdown:
The **network model** lets a record have many parents, linked by **pointers** (direct references between records).

- It handles many-to-many, which trees can't.
- Downside: you query by **following pointers by hand** in code, and new questions often mean rewriting those paths.

blocks.subTitle: Relational
blocks.markdown:
The **relational model** (1970) dropped pointers. Data is **tables of rows**, linked by shared **values** called keys.

- You say **what** you want in SQL; the database works out **how**. That style is called **declarative**.
- A **join** combines rows from two tables that share a value — so any tables can connect on the fly.

Flexible and math-backed — why it still dominates. See [relational-model-keys](relational-model-keys).

blocks.subTitle: Document & key-value
blocks.markdown:
**NoSQL** means *not only SQL* — non-relational stores that trade some guarantees for scale or flexibility.

- **Document** — stores whole **JSON documents**; each can have different fields. Good for changing app data. (MongoDB)
- **Key-value** — a big dictionary: give a **key**, get its **value** fast. Good for caches. (Redis)

blocks.subTitle: Graph & wide-column
blocks.markdown:
Two more shapes for specific jobs.

- **Graph** — data as **nodes** connected by **edges**. Walking links (friends of friends) is one cheap step instead of many joins. (Neo4j)
- **Wide-column** — very large tables spread across many machines for huge scale. (Cassandra)

Use these only when their exact strength is your problem.

Each model fixed the previous one's main limit.

<<< Image: a clean left-to-right timeline, 5 nodes, blue/grey palette, generous whitespace. Nodes in order: '1960s Hierarchical', '1970s Network', '1970s+ Relational', '1990s Object', '2000s+ NoSQL'. One arrow left to right labelled 'more flexible, more scale'. 2-3 word labels only. >>>

- Tree, then pointers, then tables, then flexible NoSQL.
- Relational stayed the center; NoSQL grew around it, it didn't replace it.

The **ER (entity-relationship) model** isn't storage — it's a **design sketch** you draw before building tables.

- **Entities** are the things (Customer, Order). **Relationships** connect them (a Customer places an Order).
- You then turn the sketch into relational tables.

More in [er-model](er-model).

Pick by the question you ask most.

- Joins and strict correctness → **relational**.
- Flexible, changing records → **document**.
- Relationships are the point → **graph**.
- Fast key lookups → **key-value**.

Start relational; switch only when the shape truly fights you.

What teams run today:

- **PostgreSQL / MySQL** — default relational.
- **MongoDB** — document.
- **Redis** — key-value cache.
- **Neo4j** — graph.

Modern setups mix them; Postgres can even store JSON documents in a column.

Common mistakes:

- **"NoSQL replaced relational."** No — it added options; relational still runs most systems.
- **"Schema-less means no design."** Document data still needs a shape; you just enforce it in code.
- **"One model for everything."** Forcing the wrong shape hurts — mix models when needed.

blocks.subTitle: SQL vs NoSQL
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: SQL vs NoSQL — when would you choose each?**

**SQL/relational** when you need correctness, joins, and flexible queries (orders, payments). **NoSQL** when you need to scale out, store changing shapes, or serve one fast lookup (catalogs, sessions).

Best answer: it's not either/or — use relational as the base and add a document store or cache where it helps.

blocks.subTitle: Database vs DBMS vs model
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Database vs DBMS vs data model?**

**Data** is raw facts. A **database** is organized data. A **DBMS** is the software that manages it (Postgres, MySQL). A **data model** is the shape it uses (relational, document).

So Postgres, a DBMS, uses the relational model to run your database.

blocks.subTitle: Why relational won
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why did relational beat the older models?**

The older models made you follow fixed pointer paths, so a new question meant rewriting code. Relational links by **values** and lets you ask **declaratively** in SQL — any join, anytime. That flexibility won.

blocks.subTitle: When a graph wins
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When does a graph database clearly win?**

When relationships are the query: friends of friends, fraud rings, dependencies. In SQL each hop is another join and it blows up; a graph walks edges directly and stays fast as the hops grow.

blocks.subTitle: Is schema-less real?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Is a "schema-less" database really schema-less?**

No — it's schema-**flexible**. The engine won't enforce fields, but your data still has a shape your code depends on. You've moved that enforcement into the app, not removed it.
